title: Beware the Belabored Anecdote
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart warns teachers and presenters against telling stories that run longer than the point requires. Only someone with Elon Musk's standing can afford a belabored anecdote; a teacher with a room of adolescents or a colleague in a department meeting cannot. He offers rules of thumb: share a story when it genuinely helps students or builds classroom culture, but do it efficiently, because every minute of anecdote is a minute students are not reading, writing, speaking or arguing. The same logic applies in meetings, where listeners have given up their time and are owed something of value. He admits he learned this the hard way and treats it as a small habit that still matters.
points: A belabored anecdote is a story longer than needed to land its point, and only the very high-status can get away with it.
In a classroom each anecdote has a price tag, paid in student time that could go to reading, writing, speaking or arguing.
The test for sharing a story in a meeting is whether it gives the listener something of value in return for their time.
Stuart wants the class to be about students getting better at the subject, not a teacher-centered show.
quotes: When we share a story to illustrate a point or a concept, and that story becomes longer than it needs to be to bring home the point, that's a belabored anecdote. When you're someone who started a rocket company that now does delivery work for NASA, then you can get away with this — go ahead, keep sharing your belabored anecdote because you're Elon Musk. But when you're teaching a classroom full of adolescents, or when you're speaking at a department meeting, you (and I) really can't.

My classroom cannot become (God forbid) the Mr. Stuart Show — it must become the Us Getting Better at World History and Life Show. Every minute listening to your anecdote is a minute that students can't spend reading, writing, speaking, or arguing.

If you think of something from your teaching practice that might prove productive for your fellow colleagues in the meeting you're in, share it — but do so efficiently. Having a pint at the bar with your colleagues is the perfect time for inefficient storytelling; sitting in a department meeting is really a poor time.

For an anecdote to be worth sharing, it must give something of value to the listener, who has just given you something of value (their time). It would be a bit rude to have someone give me their time so that they can listen to me indulge myself with an anecdote.
I've learned (and am learning) all of these the hard way, so if you struggle with the belabored or untimely anecdote, welcome to the club. It's a small thing, but the small things matter.
